You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “Uncanny Valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

entries.title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
entries.summary: As agents go mainstream, some publishers are hoping that people will pay for content tailor-made for AI—not humans.
entries.content:
Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.

Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.

“I’m kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.

Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.

“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. “We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.

Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.

Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.

What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.

“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”

At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.

“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.

The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger and acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.

Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’ reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.

While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.

Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.

Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.

Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.

Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.

“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you’re telling,” Shipper says. “And there’s always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.

“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.

As outlets eye AI agents as a new audience, another question looms: Can publishers actually make money off of this?

Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.

Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’ chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don’t want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that’s something that’s already benefiting us.”

But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.

Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.

Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”

Murphy says that Axios’ starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.

“I also try to make it a little less existentially terrifying by thinking, this isn’t the first time this has happened in media,” Murphy says. People get their news via social media, via short-form video, via podcasts. “It isn’t really AI as the audience,” Murphy adds. “It’s AI as a tool that helps us reach our audience.”

entries.title: NASA’s Oldest Martian Spacecraft Have Been Running for Decades. Here’s How
entries.summary: Two orbiters have long outlasted their expected lifespans and completely reshaped our understanding of the Red Planet, all while operating 140 million miles from Earth.
entries.content:
NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer than anyone watching their launches could have dreamed possible.

Having such a long record of observations from above the Martian surface has rewritten the story of water on the planet, past and present alike. Keeping the wizened orbiters going for so long has been possible only thanks to great engineering and constant problem solving—and a little luck. But scientists wonder whether, despite their storied legacies, Odyssey and MRO will be the last of their kind, at least for the Red Planet.

“Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed,” says Briony Horgan, a planetary scientist at Purdue University who isn’t affiliated with either mission, calling them “critical” to NASA’s overall Mars research program. Odyssey’s observations of the planet’s ice, for example, and MRO’s ability to see surface features change over time have each given scientists unprecedented insight into Mars as a vibrant planet rather than a lump of rock. Odyssey and MRO also connect humans to every NASA rover, which can’t communicate with Earth directly. It’s an impressive legacy for a pair of orbiters that were only meant to last just a few years.

Space is a notoriously harsh environment that takes luck and resilience to survive for decades. Particularly tricky is the barrage of high-energy particles hitting machinery; a powerful enough strike to a delicate enough apparatus can be fatal. And whereas engineers can keep constant tabs on satellites orbiting Earth, bandwidth to Mars is more limited—science spacecraft might only check in once or twice a week, says Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who has worked on a range of more recent Mars orbiters.

“A Mars craft has to be able to manage by itself,” he says.

Losing an instrument is bad, but losing the power or computing systems can brick the whole craft. NASA often doubles up on vital parts of a spacecraft to ensure that if something important fails, the mission can run off the spare until engineers can troubleshoot a problem.

In the MRO’s case, one challenge it’s faced is ironically due to its staying power. The orbiter determines its precise location and orientation by comparing what its cameras see with a stellar atlas onboard—with just one hiccup. “MRO is actually old enough that some of those stars have moved across the night sky—very slightly, but they have moved,” says Paul Fieseler, an engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and chief engineer for MRO. The tiny misalignments confused the spacecraft, and last year, engineers had to send up an updated map to keep MRO oriented into the future.

Odyssey’s greatest risk right now is simply running out of propellant it uses to make tiny adjustments to maintain its orientation in space. The spacecraft doesn’t have a fuel gauge–without gravity to push the fuel down, there’s no volume to measure–so NASA can’t be sure how much juice it still has. Engineers have improvised new ways to fully operate the spacecraft on just a few drops at a time in a bid to extend its life.

Experts say both spacecraft benefited from failures during NASA’s infamous “faster, better, cheaper” era. In 1999, NASA lost two missions arriving at Mars: First the Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the atmosphere, and then, just months later, the Mars Polar Lander botched its arrival and slammed into the surface. Each catastrophe, investigations determined, was caused by what might in more pedestrian realms be dubbed careless mistakes. The first was due to miscommunication between a ground system relying on imperial units and the flight system using metric, while the second was due to a software error not caught during testing.

“Those failures were very much on the mind of the team pulling together the Odyssey spacecraft,” says Glen Havens, an engineer at JPL and project and mission manager of Mars Odyssey. With those losses stinging, NASA invested more in perfecting the Odyssey and MRO spacecraft before launch, designing each to be as resilient as possible and testing every tiny component and every system configuration.

One key principle is what NASA calls “margin”—the spacecraft equivalent of carrying a snack, just in case.

“Unexpected things might happen, and you want to make sure the spacecraft will survive,” says Nilton Renno, a spaceflight engineer at the University of Michigan who hasn’t worked on either mission. MRO launched with a larger battery and more propellant than it strictly needed, Fieseler notes, and that margin is now keeping the mission going, with NASA hoping to operate it for another decade.

But orbiting Mars, it’s wise not to take anything for granted. Just last year, NASA lost the 11-year-old Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution—its youngest Red Planet orbiter—after the spacecraft unexpectedly lost power on the far side of the planet. As Odyssey and MRO continue to age, questions linger about what Mars orbiters come next for NASA.

The agency has hired Blue Origin to build a dedicated communications satellite to beam scads of data back to Earth for at least five years—but unlike its forebears, which began as science missions before turning to communications work, this orbiter will only relay signals for other spacecraft.

NASA’s Mars science agenda includes only relatively limited projects. One mission, which Lillis leads, features two orbiters currently on their way to study how the planet responds to the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun. But even he calls the mission “right on the edge of being too small to do good science.” Then, there’s Skyfall, the trio of small helicopters meant to launch aboard the first nuclear-propelled spacecraft within just two years—a shockingly rapid timeline, and for a mission with minimal ability to answer meaty research questions.

To scientists, none of these initiatives quite build on the legacy of Odyssey and MRO and may even raise the specter of the infamous Mars failures that came before. “Certainly they’re pushing for faster, cheaper,” Horgan says. “It’s going to be a lot more challenging to do good science in that environment.”

entries.title: Instagram Is a Streaming Service Now
entries.summary: Instagram’s long-form video update is more than a swipe at YouTube. It’s an attempt to capture the clip economy.
entries.content:
I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.

My Instagram Reels algorithm recently served me, along with 5 million other viewers, a brief rant from Myrick about feeling bamboozled by the health care system. Then, I spent the next hour scrolling through the show’s other snippets on Reels, loving the couple’s snarky banter. Still, I never followed the duo to a different platform to watch the full-length podcasts.

On Monday, Instagram announced plans that might have turned me into a regular listener of the show. Instagram will expand tests in the US that let creators upload long-form content up to 90 minutes and flip a video’s orientation to horizontal. Creators can also link their short clips directly back to full-length videos.

“Our belief here is that entertainment and creativity are not limited to a three-minute video,” Tessa Lyons, vice president of product at Instagram, tells WIRED. She wants to build the “best place for social entertainment” with this overhaul of Instagram video. The social media platform may soon feel like a streaming service, as more viewers watch longer videos on their big screen.

Instagram is also expanding its creator tools for turning Reels into episodic content. “We want to be able to say, ‘Wow, Reece loved episode 3. So, as soon as episode 4 drops, we've got to make sure to show it to him,’” Lyons says. This Reels feature, called “Series,” is already available for some creators in the app, and it's being tested for TV viewing as well.

Instagram is focused on the experience of watching videos on your TV. It's hunting for ways to make that TV experience feel social, like showing your connections what you’ve been watching via the Friends tab. The company also plans to turn your smartphone into a TV remote.

Lyons sees the video-focused update as avoiding one of IGTV’s core mistakes—IGTV was the company’s previous attempt at more expansive content. In that instance, many viewers desperately wanted to flip the screen. IGTV failed to connect with users, in part, because it only allowed vertical videos. Meta discontinued the app a few years after its 2018 launch.

While Instagram’s latest changes challenge YouTube’s TV dominance, they also try to leverage its current strength as a platform for clips. Bite-sized clips, often of two people sitting behind podcast microphones, feel inescapable on social media right now, with many creators using them to boost visibility. Even WIRED’s own podcast now records videos for social media clipping.

Instagram is streamlining a viewer’s potential fandom journey. Rather than viral clips and long-form content existing on different platforms, Instagram is positioning itself as a centralized experience where I can stumble on Myrick’s health care rant in the morning and then open the app on my TV later that night and get a nudge to stream the full podcast episode.

“What we're seeing right now is that a lot of great short-form content is vertical, and a lot of great long-form content is horizontal, and we have the design challenge of figuring out how to make that all work cohesively in one product,” Lyons says. “TV becomes a great destination for watching long-form, horizontal content, and mobile becomes a great place for discovering that content.”

entries.title: Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls
entries.summary: From heat maps to Signal chats to war rooms, volunteers across the US are ready to act if federal immigration agents show up on Election Day.
entries.content:
The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”

The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.

“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”

Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.

“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”

These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.

Officially, the Department of Homeland Security has said that it has no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on Election Day. “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED, but added: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”

For the past six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out possible deployments to voting locations during the midterms, even though they would be illegal under federal law. When asked in May if he would deploy the National Guard or ICE during the midterms, Trump said: “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections.”

“Why are there objections to sending ICE officers to polling places?” Todd Blanche, then acting attorney general, said in July. “Illegals can’t vote.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Some election experts simply don’t believe it will happen: “ICE and troops will not be at the polls,” David Becker, a former Justice Department trial attorney who is now head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said at a recent media briefing. “It won't happen. If it happens at all, it will be isolated. It will be accidental. It just won't happen.”

But for organizations on the ground interacting with voters in communities that have been targeted by ICE during Trump’s second term in office, the reality feels very different. Hundreds of different groups are part of the fight against possible ICE intimidation at the polls, and they are all working in coordination with each other.

“I've been up and down this state, in and out of Reno, in and out of Las Vegas, into our rural counties, and the number one question I get is about federal agents at polling locations,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, tells WIRED.

Beatriz Lopez, the executive director of Voto Latino, a group encouraging Hispanic and Latino citizens to register to vote, agrees, particularly when it comes to the communities her organization is focused on.

“We know that Latino voters are in the crosshairs of this administration because we know our electorate, our voting bloc, is what's going to shape and determine the elections of so many competitive races,” Lopez tells WIRED. “There is legitimate fear among our community.”

Lopez’s group, like many others WIRED spoke to, will be operating a war room on Election Day, with the specific goal of identifying and debunking viral disinformation that could dissuade citizens from voting. But they are also preparing for more troubling, real-world concerns.

“One of the scenarios that we're anticipating is that at the same time that we're trying to get people out to vote, there might be home raids by ICE in some of these neighborhoods, which has a real chilling effect on people,” Lopez said.

To combat this scenario, groups like 614 ICE Watch in Columbus are organizing patrols in neighborhoods near polling locations. “We send our folks in pairs or in groups. We never want to send anyone alone; we always want to have multiple people there so they can help take control of the situation,” Baiman says, adding that they have trained volunteers in a unique method of de-escalation: “If it starts to get very tense, we teach our folks to hum, to sing, to calm themselves down.”

The goal is not to interact with ICE agents but to document what they are doing so that events can be properly recorded and shared publicly. In January, just days after Alex Pretti was shot and killed in Minneapolis, more than 200,000 people logged into an “Eyes on Ice” Zoom training session, designed to teach people how to properly document ICE activities. Those skills are now being deployed during the midterm elections, Ezra Levin, cofounder of Indivisible, a group founded to stop the rise of authoritarianism in the US, tells WIRED.

On a much smaller scale, Living United for Change in Arizona has been training volunteers to become “constitutional defenders” in person, as the group prepares for next week’s vote. To track ICE activity, the group created a heat map that volunteers use to log and track ICE activity. The map is not available publicly, but WIRED was given access to the website and reviewed hundreds of recorded incidents of ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties.

Groups are also using social media to draw attention to what is happening. Last week in Sutter County, California, six ICE vehicles showed up in the parking lot of the Yuba City board of elections building, where a ballot drop box is located. Following a call from a local resident, NorCal Resist, a mutual aid organization, was able to send one of its trained volunteers and post an alert on Instagram.

“They don't like the attention, [and] when there's more community attention, they do often leave,” Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, tells WIRED.

DHS denied it was conducting immigration enforcement at a polling location, and said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against an illegal immigrant from Mexico. “ICE parked in front of a polling center—with permission from a representative of the center—while waiting for the target to exit the courthouse,” Chandler Rebel, a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.

Much of this work, however, is being done in private, a move Lopez says is necessary to protect the online infrastructure they have put in place over the course of the past two years. Levin said that Indivisible’s leadership team would be hunkered down in an Airbnb in an undisclosed location on Election Day, on alert to deploy their sizable resources wherever they are needed.

Despite the fear that pervades minority communities about what Trump and his federal agents will do next week, every group leader, activist and volunteer WIRED spoke to in recent weeks has repeated one central belief: They are prepared.

“You have all this traditional election protection infrastructure that's really, really robust, but then there is this grassroots infrastructure,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, which combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They've done all this tactical documentation training. They know how to be constitutional observers, and I'm pretty confident that when and if we have an uptick in federal enforcement at the polls, it's going to get documented really, really quickly, and it's going to be beamed out to the world that it's happening.”

entries.title: How to Hide Your Baby From the Government
entries.summary: “Sovereign citizens” think they can live beyond the reach of the state. Now the movement has influencers—and they’re selling all sorts of anarchist courses to expectant families.
entries.content:
At first blush, Kristin LaHargoue’s social media resembles that of many thirtysomething moms espousing aspirational lifestyles. To her 88,000-plus followers on Instagram, LaHargoue—a crunchy blonde living in central Utah—routinely posts her children, her husband, and herself traipsing around the globe on her account @veda.revival. There they are, standing before the Sagrada Familia, striking silly poses on a busy Tokyo street, or dancing beachside in the Philippines. In an April 2026 post soundtracked to a version of Taylor Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia,” LaHargoue wrote that she and her family have thus far traveled to over 40 countries.

Flying around the world at such a clip isn’t unusual for influencers. But LaHargoue says her children, although born in the US, travel without birth certificates or Social Security numbers. Her thinking is aligned with the sovereign citizen movement: an ever-expanding group of anti-government activists that, for almost half a century, have operated on the belief that they aren’t subject to US law. “Hot take: You don’t actually need a birth certificate to raise a thriving, traveling, fully functional child,” she writes in the same post. “Yeah … I said it. Because we are living proof of it.” By virtue of not registering her two young children’s births, she says her sons are “sovereign babies”—an oft-used hashtag, on accounts such as LaHargoue’s, to describe a child bearing alternative identification documents.

With her brand Veda Revival, LaHargoue offers a white-glove concierge service to new and expecting parents, rooted in the belief that obtaining requisite birth documents is tantamount to entering one’s children into “the jurisdiction of the US corporation.” A larger sovereign citizen movement has existed in the US for decades, with its practitioners similarly eschewing traditional government documents; acts of protest can also include tax evasion, driving without a license, and in the case of Terry Nichols—domestic terrorism. But the rise of influencers selling an alternative means of obtaining a passport, and the idea that babies can be sovereign, represents a new, digitally native outgrowth of this ideology.

For $497, LaHargoue sells a bundle that includes videos and templates for parents to obtain passports for their children based on “nationality” versus “citizenship,” with detailed instructions so they might respond confidently during “interactions with agents of the matrix.” Those seeking something more intensive can pay $997 for “hand-holding,” meaning that LaHargoue will personally guide them in navigating this divergent route. (LaHargoue declined WIRED’s request for an interview, citing the forthcoming birth of her third child.)

LaHargoue, who says she has worked with over 1,000 parents to obtain passports for their sovereign babies, is one of a growing cohort of influencers working in the unregulated industry that’s now selling this self-taught knowledge. One “family legacy architect” named Minister Dionne, known for broadcasting missives to her 125,000 Instagram followers about how registering one’s child makes them “wards of the state,” offers “Status Correction FastTrack Bundles” for securing noncitizen national passports (for as much as $555). LaHargoue also offers an affiliate program for those who want to make a commission of 15 to 20 percent by successfully selling her sovereign baby services.

It’s impossible to quantify how many sovereign babies currently live in the US, given their parents’ feelings about record-taking. (According to one oft-cited estimate, 100,000 to 300,000 people identify as sovereign citizens, although it's hard to know exactly because of the nature of the movement.) But Adam Bojak, a family law attorney in western New York who is currently on the ballot for the New York state legislature, says that he’s seen an uptick in cases involving sovereign children. In decades past, he’d have maybe one client per year who’d vacate or even try to reject formal identification documents for their children; lately, that’s increased to a half dozen a year, a phenomenon he suspects is linked to the “psychic break” that happened during Covid. “So many of these things are downstream from the aftereffects of that,” he says. “Just where people were ripped apart socially and physically from each other, emotionally. [It’s a rupture] that leads into this idea that everybody’s out for themselves.”

Remote learning during the pandemic also transformed education. Homeschooling rates surged in the early 2020s and remain high: The National Home Education Research Institute estimated earlier this year that 3.4 million children in the US are homeschooled—a number that is almost certainly underreported—compared to 1.4 million back in 2003. Tess Ulrey, executive director of the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, is unsurprised that the sovereign baby movement has risen in tandem with homeschooling rates, as homeschooling can become an inadvertent gateway into sovereign thinking. Some parents might pull their child out of school and “get tied up in this ideology of like, ‘Well, it is my right to do whatever I want. Well, why would the government be tracking that?’” she says.

Indeed, peppered between posts name-checking Rumi and denouncing circumcision, LaHargoue encourages parents to reject conventional education systems. In her July appearance on the Born Free Method podcast, LaHargoue spoke about her belief that the US school system is connected to a larger government plot that, by virtue of the birth certificate, “contracts” children as human capital. “That school system is now teaching them how to be a good worker,” she said. “Let’s shuffle them right down this path.”

A recent rise in “world schooling,” or rooting a child’s instruction in travel rather than curricula, is similarly linked with the sovereign baby movement. Jemila Moore, a doula based in South Carolina, lives nomadically with her partner and four young children. Her three youngest kids have neither birth certificates nor Social Security numbers. Moore, who swears by world schooling, wanted to ensure that her children had the ability to travel with passports. Wherever her family may be, Moore accompanies her children to local public libraries to read and do math exercises. “There's nothing greater than children being able to learn about other countries while actually witnessing those countries and their culture, and let those countries tell their history versus just reading it in a textbook,” she says. “I think that it really makes a difference on our development as people and how we view the world.”

While sovereign babies are bred on the grounds of government suspicion, sovereign-minded parents still “want to travel under the banner of the United States of America without actually being subject to the United States of America,” says Bojak. “Like George Costanza said, ‘We’re living in a society,’ and these are the barriers you have to clear to live in a society.” Rob Finch, a North Carolina–based consultant who trains law enforcement officers to engage with sovereign citizens who don’t believe they are subject to the law, says this ideology is "not fact-based," adding: “You've got a lot of opportunistic people selling these packages of ‘Keep your kid off the grid, here's how you do it.’”

Without clearing these barriers, experts worry that sovereign babies are far more likely to fall through societal cracks and live insular lives. Most will be unable to drive, find jobs, or even secure housing without the crucial documents one needs to move through the world.

Birth certificates and Social Security numbers represent a relatively new standard for identification in the US. During the colonial period, American churches primarily kept birth records. But when millions of Europeans immigrated to the States in the 19th century, reformers became concerned about rising poverty rates, overpopulation, and the spread of epidemics in densely populated urban areas. In a bid to better understand public health, the US Census Bureau developed standardized certificates and began tracking births, though not every state followed suit. The process became more nationally standardized around the 1930s, and firmly de rigueur during World War II, when some factories would only employ US citizens as part of the war effort.

To some sovereign citizens, it’s no coincidence that birth certificates became rote in the 1930s, the same decade FDR signed an executive order replacing gold as the backing standard for US currency. Proponents of the “straw man theory,” a central premise in sovereign ideology, hold that when parents take out a birth certificate and Social Security number for their child, the government then opens an account in their name and uses them, in the absence of gold, as human capital to back US debt. This bogus theory is often invoked by sovereign citizens who, say, get pulled over for driving without a license, as a way of justifying their actions: They believe that every individual has two separate personas—a legal entity that is bound by the government, and themselves—and that laws thus don’t apply to them as individuals. To date, no US court has ever sided with sovereign citizens invoking these arguments, says family law attorney Christopher C. Melcher: “There's no legal basis for what they're saying, but they say it with enough conviction and consistency that they hope they can get away with it.”

The modern sovereign citizens movement has its roots in a hate-fueled paramilitary cohort called Posse Comitatus (Latin for “power of the county”). In the 1970s, an ex-Army lieutenant colonel turned “minister” named William Potter Gale founded the group, hinged on racist and antisemetic beliefs, in Southern California. Gale believed in a “citizen’s government” that would exact justice in its own way; throughout the decade, his followers violently detained and assaulted an IRS worker and attempted to “indict” a judge. When an agricultural crisis gripped the US, his conspiracy-driven ideas spread throughout the country. Posse Comitatus’ anti-government tactics, which include not paying taxes, later spread into a larger sovereign citizens’ movement, which now has dozens of different factions and chapters in various states. One such group is the American State Nationals, who align with sovereign citizen ideology but distance themselves from the moniker because of the movement’s white supremacist origins. ASNs believe one can obtain a noncitizen national passport that, by virtue of having a certain number of stars on it, gives them limited diplomatic immunity. Some even sell bundles on social media that allow people, for several hundred dollars, to exit their “contract” with the US government through a passport based on nationality rather than citizenship.

Beyond a skepticism of the US government, the parents of sovereign babies are difficult to pin down. They typically do not align with any one political party or religious group. While some live more holistic and off-grid lifestyles, and an overlap does exist between sovereignty practitioners and ardent anti-vaxers, it wouldn’t be accurate to say that this is a strain of the Make America Healthy Again movement, either. Rather than having one centralized leader or a physical community, the sovereign baby phenomenon is more akin to a vast constellation, people connected by the belief that by applying for a birth certificate and Social Security number, they are “binding” their children with the “United States corporation,” as LaHargoue likes to put it. In a series of videos included in Veda Revival’s “Born Free Blueprint,” LaHargoue argues that sovereign babies are “ushering in a new era of freedom.” (These videos are free, but before purchasing and viewing LaHargoue’s more in-depth guides, all clients are required to upload a passport/ID and sign an agreement accepting the terms of entering her member community—which threatens legal action if one does not use her information with “integrity and benevolence.”)

The US Department of State requires evidence of citizenship before approving a passport. If one doesn’t have a primary document (such as a birth certificate), the agency accepts several forms of secondary evidence, including a delayed birth certificate and a Letter of No Record—which must be issued by the state and include public record documents such as a hospital birth certificate, baptism records, school records, or a census record. Those hewing to sovereign thinking tend to go with another option: a family Bible containing written inscriptions denoting the births and deaths of relatives. Melcher says it’s difficult, but not impossible, for those born on US soil to obtain secondary evidence that’s “sufficient to convince the State Department to issue a passport, based on them claiming that they were born in a state or territory, without a birth certificate.”

A woman living in Texas, whom I’ll call Deborah, purchased an instructional video from LaHargoue’s catalog and says she was able to obtain a passport for her infant—sans birth certificate—by submitting baptism records, a family Bible, an affidavit confirming that she had indeed given birth to him, and a formal announcement in a local newspaper announcing his birth. She notarized each of these documents and sent them certified through the mail. After an extensive back and forth, she said the office eventually approved the passport. “I opted for the passport route because that is a way of announcing, ‘Hey, I have this child,’” she says. “I'm claiming parental rights and backing them with the paperwork they'll need to make whatever choices they want in the future.”

In recent years, parents have stumbled into the sovereign baby movement through online rabbit holes, especially on Instagram, Telegram, Facebook, and Reddit. The confluence of factors that has given way to the sovereign baby movement—including the ubiquity of influencers, the isolating aftermath of Covid, skepticism of the medical establishment, and waning trust in the government—feels utterly of this time. Yet this phenomenon clashes against another tension: the Trump administration’s brutality toward immigrants and visible show of deporting people out of the US. At a moment when undocumented immigrants, green card holders, asylum seekers, and citizens are being shuttled to remote countries with little legal recourse, it’s striking that parents of sovereign children—of babies born in the US—have consciously stacked the odds against themselves and their kids.

“We shouldn't discount the fact that there's a guy in the Oval Office now, for the second time, who doesn't believe any rules pertain to him, and he's actually proven that over and over again that he doesn't have to follow laws,” Bojak, the attorney, says. “He doesn't have to follow court orders. And so if he doesn't, why the hell should any of the rest of us?”

Others arrive in other ways entirely: Deborah learned about sovereign citizen ideology—and later declined to get her toddler a birth certificate—after she’d accrued over $2,000 in speeding tickets. (She rejects the term "sovereign citizen” and claims it’s a slur; instead, she prefers to say she is "maximizing potential freedom” for her child.) “I ended up doing this deep dive from just having, honestly, a totally delusional idea of, ‘I'm not gonna pay these,’” she says. Some, like Zoe Durant, got here through in-person conversations with a doula, a midwife, or another professional birth attendant who usually helps new parents complete standard paperwork.

In 2016, while studying engineering in college, Durant was working as a bottle server and promotional model in Nevada. Several months after giving birth to her first child that same year, Durant and her partner traded the neon gleam of casinos for an offgrid solar farm mere miles away from Kilauea, one of the world’s most active volcanoes. She’s a “first-generation farmer” of grapefruits, bananas, lilikoi, and lychee crops in the remote Hawaiian jungle, posting dispatches on Instagram under the name @junglefairyfarm. (They have since moved to a less harsh location).

Early into building their Big Island home, in 2021, Durant found out she was pregnant with her second child. When she learned that her partner couldn’t accompany her to requisite appointments because of Covid, Durant eschewed a hospital birth altogether. Instead, she found a midwife who helped deliver her daughter in a birthing pool at home. When it was time to consider her newborn’s birth certificate and Social Security number application, Durant consulted her midwife. “She was like, ‘Well, there's families that I work with who don't do that,’” Durant says. “And I was like, ‘Oh, tell me more.’”

The midwife, Durant explained, told her that she’d helped several parents who identified as sovereign. Intrigued, and recalling how she’d felt pushed to sign these papers after her first child’s hospital birth, Durant chewed over the alternative the midwife had told her about. “It seems like something that [my daughter] could do later on if she wanted to consent to that, and it also helps protect her identity,” Durant reasoned. “In the future, she's not going to worry about someone stealing her Social Security number. And honestly, the way the economy is, I don't even know if Social Security is going to be around when she's old enough.”

But Durant worried that without documents like a birth certificate and a Social Security card, her child might run into hurdles if she wished to live a normal life. Durant instead applied for a passport for her daughter, submitting various secondary documents. At one point, Durant says, a passport agent told her that the office couldn’t grant her the document because she didn’t have hard proof of her child’s birth. Durant then sent the official a photo of herself sitting in the shallow birthing pool with her newborn, telling them, “This is the only evidence I have of the birth—because it was a sovereign birth.” These are “my beliefs,” she added, “sorry if you don’t like it.” She says the birth photo worked, and the passport office eventually sent the document along; all told, it took about six months.

Last year, Durant wrote and self-published a book, Opting Out: A Parent's Guide to a Barcode-Free Birth and Keeping Your Child Off the Grid: How to Protect Your Child's Identity and Secure Their Future Outside the State’s System. At a little under $20 per copy, it’s not the main source of the content creator/model’s income—she’s sold a few hundred copies thus far, she estimates—but Durant says that’s secondary to how “passionate” she feels about the subject. “I think a lot of parents are just trying to take back power because the government is getting a little bit overzealous with their control,” she says. One chapter of Durant’s book is dedicated solely to dealing with Child Protective Services, should the agency inquire about why one’s child does not have a birth certificate. In it, she writes: “Take a deep breath. Stand your ground. You have done your research. They were not taking your child. In that moment you realized something. The birth certificate was not just paperwork. It is permission, permission for the government to track you. To control you and intervene in your family's life whenever they see fit.”

Durant’s beliefs diverge from the mainstream sovereign baby movement, which is intertwined with free birthing—a separate, largely influencer-led movement that advocates for giving birth without medical intervention. In 2024, 1.5 percent of births in the US were free births, a number that tripled from 2004. (Durant had assistance during her home birth and believes in seeking out traditional medicine for “life-saving care”; she has been undergoing chemotherapy for a stage IV colon cancer diagnosis.) Free birthers can also opt out of prenatal care altogether, in what’s known as a “wild pregnancy.” LaHargoue, a vocal proponent of the Free Birth movement, has posted about her appearance on the Free Birth Society Podcast alongside Reels about traveling without these documents.

Marisse Vista, 34, first learned about sovereignty during the pandemic, when she was newly single and pregnant. She felt alone, save for an online “village of women” whom Vista credits with helping her “unearth a lot of things that didn't align with what I had known to be true.” After one woman told her that she believed “the birth certificate was a [government] bond,” Vista began questioning other “mainstream things,” like vaccinating her children. When Vista became pregnant with her second child, she decided to free-birth at an Airbnb after “binging” the FBS podcasts. After she decided not to obtain traditional birth documents for her infant, she started poking around online to find alternate routes to getting a passport.

By that point, Vista, a first-generation Filipina who grew up in Spring, Texas, had launched a Facebook community for like-minded sovereign mothers. When Vista mentioned in the group that she’d been trying to get her head around the alternative passport process, someone brought up Veda’s name. Vista bought LaHargoue’s step-by-step course to ensure that she had the requisite documents before going to the passport office in Waco. LaHargoue became her “echo chamber to make sure that I was doing it like fully right, because I had done all this research alone,” Vista says. “It was just a confirmation that, like, all my research was correct.”

When she became pregnant with her third child, Vista had “a pain-free, orgasmic, Frank breech free birth,” meaning that the baby emerges from the birth canal buttocks-first. The experience led Vista to help people conceive their “spirit babies” and birth them as sovereign parents. Under the banner of her brand La Souveraine Mere, her services range from a digital guide to “understanding how spirit babies communicate, what they need energetically before they can land, and how to align your womb space with their frequency” ($44) to a “Sovereign Conception Program” that includes “Spinal Energetics, frequency work, ancestral clearing, and womb activation woven into a container that treats your body as the oracle it already is” ($5,555).

Once these expectant parents get into Vista’s “world,” as she describes, “then I start to talk about, like, ‘Once you have the baby, what are you going to do? You're going to steward them. You're going to make sure that … their custodian isn't the government,’ and so we then talk about birth certificates and Social Security numbers.”

A bone-deep distrust of the medical establishment—and, in some cases, traumatic experiences—is another common gateway into free-birthing and, then, the sovereign baby movement. Moore, the former nursing assistant who studied public health in college, says she wasn’t expecting to feel “very pressured” to get an induction until she went into labor at a hospital. “When I was like, ‘Hey, since I'm already contracting, can we not do the induction? Can I just let my body go naturally?’” she says. “They're like, ‘Well, the doctor put the order in. We're just gonna do it.’” In hindsight, Moore wishes she had "advocated for herself more” in that moment. “My body was probably already doing what was necessary for me, and the induction just made my labor process a little bit more challenging than what it is actually with the natural flow.” Moore says it caused her to reflect on the disparities that women of color face when delivering children, and later informed her decision to free-birth her other kids.

There is an indisputable maternal health crisis in this country, and especially among women of color. But experts warn that free-birthing carries a heightened risk of complications, and the practice has come under intense scrutiny after infants and parents alike have died from the complications of unassisted birth. Sovereign baby influencers may risk further sowing distrust by advocating for risky, radical procedures without any prenatal care or medical professionals—particularly to those who might already be more vulnerable—by alleging that physicians are cogs in a bigger birth-certificate conspiracy. “They’ve tricked us into hiring licensed providers,” LaHargoue says in a video titled “Who’s Child Is It Really? The Truth About Birth Certificates & Legal Fiction.” “They’ve tricked us into believing that birth is even a medical event.”

“I’ve been saving this cigarette,” Sarah Ashley Townsend tells me over Zoom one June afternoon. She’s sitting in her home in Maryland, near the Susquehanna River. The windows are open. “I think that’s the hardest part to talk about,” the 43-year-old says, lighting the end of the smoke. Townsend is referring to the moment she became aware that she’d been raised differently.

Shortly before her birth, Townsend’s mother tumbled down the sovereign-ideology-aligned rabbit hole via a neighbor, who convinced her to not give birth at a hospital and to refuse paperwork. “I was not given a Social Security number, because she was going to do this all outside the boundaries of society now,” Townsend says. Vaccines were verboten, and she and her siblings lived consciously isolated from others in their community.

When her father’s family intervened and lobbied to send Townsend to school, the 5-year-old walked into kindergarten “thinking that I started school with everyone else, and I did not,” she says, her voice breaking. “I thought it was the first day of school, and apparently it was the last month of school. They made fun of me because I couldn't tie my shoes … and they all asked if I was from another planet.” Townsend’s mother would pack her inappropriate lunches or fight over signing papers that would have allowed her child to buy a meal: “She didn’t want me to have their tainted food,” she says. “She would blame us for subscribing to their system, because she didn't think we should have to be there anyway.”

Townsend considers herself fortunate that her father, while distant, advocated for her. One day he showed up at Townsend’s elementary school, and the pair walked to a medical clinic; he quietly ensured that she received vaccinations without her mother knowing. After her parents divorced, Townsend’s mother moved her and her sister around constantly, choosing off-grid places where they sometimes lived without power for months. Townsend’s father would ship her boxes with plushies and gift cards hidden inside, which she would use to buy clothes. Her dad would tuck novels into these packages with words underlined, a secret code telling her she was loved, and that she needed to stay strong.

When Townsend was 16, she tried to apply for a driver’s license and was repeatedly denied on account of her inconsistent birth and medical history. She approached her music and theater teachers for help: “How do I be an adult … how do I go do things I'm supposed to do?” she remembers asking them.

She believed she had her documents straightened out by the time she turned 18. But Townsend kept running into hurdles when she tried to join her husband’s health insurance shortly afterward. Giving birth a year later became its own kind of hell. “Do you know what happened when I gave birth to my son? All of his paperwork got kicked back,” she says, because the office said it couldn’t find evidence of her own birth. “My son's birth certificate had to be amended twice. I'm a week postpartum, 22 years old, running all over town with my husband getting notarized documents,” she says. “All I want is for my kid to have … of all the things in the world, a Social Security number and a birth certificate from the get-go.”

More than two decades on, Townsend is still haunted because she lacked a birth certificate and a Social Security number earlier in life. “As an adult, you can't have a fucking normal existence, ever, because you always have to go through a routine that will remind you that no one cared, and that you were some pawn in a weird fucking game that will affect you for the rest of your life,” she says. “And like, yes, I'm a valid citizen. I live here. I am a person. I exist.”

entries.title: Is an Under-Sink Reverse Osmosis System Worth It? Benefits, Costs, and Drawbacks
entries.summary: The Waterdrop X12 improved the taste of my tap water, but reverse osmosis comes with costs beyond the purchase price.
entries.content:
That funny taste in your tap water may be a harmless nuisance—or it may be cause for serious concern. Either way, you can do something about it by installing a reverse osmosis (RO) water filtration system in your home.

Stand-alone RO systems and pitchers sit on your countertop and generally require manual refilling from the tap. You’ll save space and avoid the hassle of constantly refilling the unit by installing an under-sink or under-counter model that connects directly to your plumbing lines. Either way, RO systems aren’t cheap. But for some homeowners, they may be an invaluable investment.

Featured in this Article

What Is Reverse Osmosis?

Osmosis is the movement of molecules—usually water—through a semipermeable membrane that blocks larger particles like salts and sugars from passing through. After osmosis, the concentration of particles on both sides of the membrane ends up in equilibrium. It’s how plants get water from the soil, and it’s how your kidneys filter junk out of your blood.

While osmosis is a spontaneous phenomenon that happens naturally, reverse osmosis requires pressure to force water through a membrane in the other direction, effectively removing all of those compounds from the water to render it pure. It’s how salt is removed from seawater to make it drinkable, and it’s one way tap water can be purified in your home.

RO differs considerably from traditional filtration systems, which rely on physical barriers, typically activated carbon, to manually capture particles that pass through. Eventually, these filters become saturated with sediments and other matter and have to be replaced. While carbon filters are fairly blunt, able to capture larger particles of at least 0.1 microns in size, RO systems have a much finer-grained membrane that captures contaminants on a microscopic level (typically down to 0.0001 microns).

Carbon filters can make your water taste and smell better, but with RO you are getting much, much cleaner water than what that inexpensive Brita filter can muster. (That said, RO can’t capture everything, and carbon filters are still useful for capturing certain volatile organic compounds through adsorption. Most RO systems also have an additional carbon filtration system included.)

Note that two types of RO systems are available: Tanked RO systems filter water slowly (albeit passively, without electricity) and sequester it in a (rather large) tank under your sink. Today, tankless RO systems are more popular, processing water on demand but requiring electricity to keep things flowing expeditiously. Tankless systems are considerably more expensive due to their inherent complexity.

What Are the Real Risks of Contaminants in Water Today?

“US tap water is safe for most people most of the time,” says John Voll, an industrial water treatment veteran and the founder of Tap & Air, a website that monitors water and air quality for hundreds of municipalities. “The problems are local, not universal.”

The first step to understanding your personal risk is to gauge whether your own water is up to snuff by simply looking up its most recent data report online. The Safe Drinking Water Act requires community water systems to publish an annual report on the quality of water they’re delivering, due by July 1 each year.

These are heady documents, so to keep things simple, Voll says to keep your eye on three key pollutant metrics: lead, nitrate or arsenic, and PFAS (so-called forever chemicals popular in nonstick cookware and other products). While the first two are serious issues, they’re fairly rare today. PFAS, however, are a particularly significant problem across the country. Voll says that 98 of the 200 largest US cities have at least one PFAS compound detected in their water supply. Reverse osmosis systems can handle them—as well as lead and other compounds. Carbon filters usually can’t.

“Most people don't need RO,” Voll says, “but some households clearly do, and the way to tell is to read your own water report first.”

What Are the Drawbacks of Using an RO System?

RO systems come with a host of downsides, but most are related in some fashion to cost.

  • RO wastes water: The particulars of RO technology have historically meant it requires a large amount of unprocessed tap water to create a small amount of purified water, sometimes up to 4 gallons or more of tap to 1 gallon of clean water (called the pure-to-drain ratio). In recent years that number has dramatically shifted, with 4 gallons of tap water producing up to 3 gallons of clean water, or a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio.
  • Filters are costly: RO systems can require up to six different filtration cartridges that must be replaced every year or two, depending on use. Much like printer ink, these costs can be easily overlooked when making your initial purchase. Plan to spend $50 to $200 annually on replacement cartridges, but check prices before you buy.
  • RO can strip “good” minerals from your water: Calcium, magnesium, and potassium are all unable to pass through the RO membrane. RO systems also remove fluoride from your water, which many users may not desire and which dentists abhor. Some RO systems can remineralize water and/or raise the pH level of the processed water thanks to additional cartridges—but these, of course, mean further expense on replaceables.
  • Plan for professional installation (and additional financial outlays): I try not to DIY too much when there’s even a remote potential for a water leak, so I get a plumber involved for installations like these. And since most RO systems require their own faucet, you’ll need to prepare to have a new hole drilled into your countertop for your tap if you don’t already have one available.

Do You Need an Under-Sink RO System?

Based on my analysis of my city’s water report, no I don’t really need an RO system, as there’s nothing hazardous to worry about. However, as the linked report notes, our water supplier uses chloramine as a disinfectant, and drinking that chloramine-treated water straight from the tap has a slight but noticeable, off-putting taste. This is exacerbated by the extreme hardness of the water; this part of Texas is basically built on top of nothing but limestone, and the resulting amount of calcium carbonate in the water can add a slightly bitter flavor, as well.

For me, RO is all about the way the water tastes. Any lingering contaminants that are removed along the way are just a bonus.

I tested the Waterdrop X12 for this story, hiring a plumber to remove a well-aged unit under the sink and replace it with this more capable one. The job was done in less than an hour.

Under-sink RO filters are separate from your existing plumbing, and most use three color-coded lengths of tubing to tie into it. One connects to your incoming water supply through an adapter valve, one clips into your wastewater drainpipe via an included fitting, and one connects to the faucet. I am confident I could have made these connections on my own—especially since I was replacing an existing system—but I’ve seen how even a small water leak can lead to devastating problems and was happy for the peace of mind that professional oversight supplied.

Once installed and powered up, the X12 launches a 35-minute priming process designed to flush the filters before first use. It seems like an awfully long time for the sink to run, and it is. If you have some way to capture and use all this extra water, plan ahead to collect it. After the session completed (it stops automatically), I was ready to start sipping from the tap.

The X12 is exceedingly simple to use. Tap the LED-equipped button on top of the faucet to start or stop the flow of water, or twist the same button to dial in the number of ounces you want to dispense (up to 999) before depressing it. This way, you can drop your 64-ounce Stanley Quencher in the sink and walk away without having to wait around or worry about an overflow, with a digital timer first offering a measurement of your water’s current TDS (total dissolved solids), then counting down the ounces as they’re dispensed. The good news is that you won’t have to wait long: The X12 blasts water out of its spigot faster than my kitchen sink does—a far cry from the sad dribble of H2O my old RO system provided.

The unit can also be switched into one of two alternate operating modes, including an energy-saving mode (which quiets the device) and “flow mode,” which is designed for high-use households. Both require pressing certain button combinations on the filtration unit. I have used the device in all three modes, and (contrary to other reviews I’ve seen) I’ve never found it to be noisy at all, even though it’s located just 20 feet from my bed.

As for the water, it tastes great. The remineralization feature and pH adjustment (to about 7.5, which I confirmed with a pH test strip) give the water a pleasant tang while avoiding any harshness or chemical flavors. Unfortunately it doesn’t come out particularly cold, which means having to add non-RO ice to the glass to chill it down. First-world problem, I know.

I was especially pleased to discover that the X12 has one of the best water efficiency rates in the business, with a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio (3 gallons of pure water production to 1 gallon lost). Replacement filters (three are needed in total) are sold à la carte for $30 to $160 each.

For an even more powerful version—ideal for larger households—consider the Waterdrop X16, which uses the same cartridges and offers the same features as the X12. WIRED editor Kat Merck, whose municipal water supply does contain PFAS, has had one installed for a year and a half without any maintenance or reliability issues.
